title: How to export Google Trends data to CSV/JSON without an API key (2026)
author: CleanData Labs
summary: Google Trends is one of the best free signals for demand: is a product category growing, which country searches for it most, and which queries are rising right now. Getting that data out of Google Trends is harder. The website gives you one small CSV per chart, and doing that by hand for 50 keywords is a lost afternoon. This guide covers why exporting is awkward in 2026, how to export Trends data to CSV, JSON or Excel without code, and how to do the same from Python. The problem: no open API, and pytrends is archived There is still no generally available official API. In July 2025 Google announced a Google Trends API alpha . As of October 2026 it is still application-only: the page asks developers to apply as alpha testers, and Google has said it is onboarding a small group. If you have a research use case it is worth applying, but you can't count on access. pytrends, the popular unofficial library, is no longer maintained. The GeneralMills/pytrends repository is archived, and the last PyPI release (4.9.2) is from April 2023. It can still work, but you are on your own with Google's frequent 429 Too Many Requests responses, changes to the internal endpoints, and proxy rotation. Manual CSV downloads don't scale. Each chart on trends.google.com has its own download button, and every file has its own header layout. One thing to remember whatever tool you use: Google Trends values are a relative index from 0 to 100 , not search volumes. 100 is the peak popularity within that request (those keywords, that region, that time range). Change the comparison and the numbers change. Option: a hosted Google Trends scraper For this walkthrough I'll use Google Trends Explorer , an Actor on the Apify platform (disclosure: built by CleanData Labs). It reads the same public data you see on trends.google.com and returns: interest over time (with isPartial flags and per-keyword averages), interest by region (country, state, city or US metro), related queries and related topics (top and rising, with a numeric growthPercent and an isBreakout flag), daily Trending Now searches per country. It retries rate-limited requests with a new session (and a new proxy IP when Apify Proxy is enabled), and failed queries are reported in the dataset instead of silently disappearing. Pricing: $0.0025 per result, where one result is a complete data block (for example, a full 12-month timeline or a full region table), not one row per date. Error rows and "no data" rows are free, and Apify adds a $0.00005 Actor start fee per run. Apify's free plan includes $5 of monthly credit, so you can try it without paying. Step-by-step: export Google Trends data in Apify Console Open the Actor page and click Try for free . Sign in or create a free Apify account. In Keywords / search terms , enter your terms, e.g. electric bike and e-scooter . You can also paste a full chart link into Google Trends URLs . The keywords, country, time range, category and property are read from the URL. Turn on Compare keywords together if you want the keywords on one shared 0–100 scale (up to 5 per comparison, like on the website). Leave it off to get a separate chart for each keyword. Set Countries / regions (e.g. US , GB , or US-CA for California; leave empty for worldwide) and a Time range , such as Past 12 months . Use Custom time range for exact dates ( 2025-01-01 2025-12-31 ). Tick the data you need: Interest over time , Interest by region , Related queries (top + rising) , Related topics (top + rising) . For daily trending searches, add country codes to Trending Now countries . If you plan to open the file in Excel or Google Sheets, turn on Flatten output (CSV / Sheets friendly) . Each date or region then becomes its own row instead of a nested array. The price stays the same, because billing counts data blocks, not rows. Click Start . A small run like this usually finishes in well under a minute. Open the Output tab and export as JSON, CSV, Excel , XML or HTML. Every row includes a trendsUrl , so you can open the same chart on trends.google.com and check it. What the output looks like Here is a shortened interest-over-time row from a real run (US, past 12 months, the two keywords compared): { "type" : "interest_over_time" , "keywords" : [ "electric bike" , "e-scooter" ], "geo" : "US" , "timeRange" : "today 12-m" , "timeline" : [ { "date" : "Oct 26 – Nov 1, 2025" , "timestamp" : 1761436800 , "isPartial" : false , "electric bike" : 13 , "e-scooter" : 0 }, { "date" : "Nov 2 – 8, 2025" , "timestamp" : 1762041600 , "isPartial" : false , "electric bike" : 16 , "e-scooter" : 1 } ], "averages" : { "electric bike" : 31 , "e-scooter" : 1 }, "pointCount" : 53 } And one entry from the "rising" list of a related-queries row from the same run: { "rank" : 2 , "query" : "yozma" , "value" : 4100 , "formattedValue" : "+4,100%" , "isBreakout" : false , "growthPercent" : 4100 } "Breakout" entries (growth over 5,000%) come with isBreakout: true and growthPercent: null , so you can filter them without parsing strings. Python example with apify-client To automate this, install the official client ( pip install apify-client ) and get your API token from Settings → API & Integrations in Apify Console. I tested this with apify-client 3.4: import os from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ " APIFY_TOKEN " ]) run_input = { " keywords " : [ " electric bike " , " e-scooter " ], " compareKeywords " : True , " geos " : [ " US " ], " timeRange " : " today 12-m " , " interestOverTime " : True , " interestByRegion " : True , " regionResolution " : " REGION " , " relatedQueries " : True , } run = client . actor ( " cleandata-labs/google-trends-explorer " ). call ( run_input = run_input ) for item in client . dataset ( run . default_dataset_id ). iterate_items (): if item [ " type " ] == " interest_over_time " : for point in item [ " timeline " ]: print ( point [ " date " ], point [ " electric bike " ], point [ " e-scooter " ]) That run returned four results: one timeline, one table of 51 US regions, and one related-queries list per keyword. To get a CSV file directly, call the dataset items endpoint with format=csv , for example https://api.apify.com/v2/datasets/<DATASET_ID>/items?format=csv . Combine it with flattenOutput: true for clean columns. With the JavaScript client the same call is client.actor("cleandata-labs/google-trends-explorer").call(input) . Tips for comparing keywords Compare in one request. Values from separate requests are each scaled to their own peak, so "62" in one chart and "62" in another are not comparable. Put the terms in one comparison ( compareKeywords: true ). Use an anchor term for more than 5 keywords. Split them into groups of 4 plus one shared reference keyword, then rescale each group by the anchor's values. Watch the last data point. Points with isPartial: true cover a period that hasn't ended yet and usually look lower than they will end up. Use topics for ambiguous words. Turn on Keyword / topic suggestions to get Google's topic IDs (e.g. /m/... ). Topics group spellings and languages; plain search terms don't. Look at the scale. In the run above, "e-scooter" averaged 1 next to "electric bike". That doesn't mean nobody searches for it. Next to a much bigger term, small ones get rounded down toward 0. Tips for regional data Use ISO codes in Countries / regions : DE for Germany, US-TX for Texas. Region resolution controls the breakdown: COUNTRY (worldwide), REGION (states/provinces), CITY , or DMA (US metro areas). Keep Only regions with data on (the default) to drop regions where Google reports nothing. Region values are relative too: 100 is the region with the highest share of searches for the term, not the most searches. For more than about 20 queries per run, enable Apify Proxy (residential works best), because Google rate-limits busy IP addresses. Wrapping up Until Google's official API is widely available, you can choose between doing it by hand, maintaining a scraper yourself, or using a hosted one. If you just need clean JSON or CSV for a list of keywords, a hosted Actor like Google Trends Explorer is quick to set up. You can schedule it in Apify Console or connect it to Google Sheets, Make, Zapier or n8n. Whatever tool you use, the data is the public, aggregated information Google shows on its website. Check Google's terms and the rules that apply to your use.

title: cURL to Code: Convert API Requests to Python, JavaScript, Go & PHP Without Leaking Secrets
author: Rashid Salimov
summary: When integrating third-party APIs, debugging webhooks, or replicating browser network requests, curl commands from Chrome DevTools or documentation are the universal starting point. However, manually rewriting a 15-line cURL request with nested headers, query parameters, multipart payloads, and basic/bearer authentication into native code is tedious and error-prone. Worse, pasting commands with active Authorization: Bearer <token> or Cookie: session=... into random online converter websites sends your production credentials to remote servers where they may be logged or cached. The Client-Side Solution: cURL to Code Converter To protect your secrets, the cURL to Code Converter on Digital Vault PRO runs 100% inside your browser using client-side JavaScript. No bytes ever leave your machine. How It Works Paste any cURL command — whether copied directly from Chrome Network tab ("Copy as cURL (bash)"), Postman, or official documentation: curl -X POST 'https://api.example.com/v1/orders' \ -H 'Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1Ni...' \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"order_id": 1042, "status": "confirmed"}' The converter parses flags ( -X , -H , -d , --data-raw , -u , -F , -k ), tokenizes arguments, and generates idiomatic code for: 1. ' , ' Content-Type ' : ' application/json ' }, body : JSON . stringify ({ order_id : 1042 , status : ' confirmed ' }) }); const data = await response . json (); console . log ( data ); 2. Go ( net/http ) package main import ( "bytes" "io" "log" "net/http" ) func main () { payload := [] byte ( `{"order_id": 1042, "status": "confirmed"}` ) req , err := http . NewRequest ( "POST" , "https://api.example.com/v1/orders" , bytes . NewBuffer ( payload )) if err != nil { log . Fatal ( err ) } req . Header . Do ( req ) if err != nil { log . Fatal ( err ) } defer resp . Body . Close () body , _ := io . ReadAll ( resp . Body ) log . Println ( string ( body )) } 4. title: The LiteLLM incident check you shouldn't run with Python — and the scanner I built for it
author: XM Yang
summary: On Oct 21, 2026, LiteLLM disclosed that its v1.107.0 release had been compromised and published to PyPI, Docker Hub, and GHCR before being contained. The part of the official response steps that stuck with me: in an affected environment, any Python start re-runs the implant . So the vendor tells you not to begin with pip install or pip show on a suspect box. The first-pass checks are file and metadata checks, done from the shell, by hand: - Is litellm pinned to exactly 1.107.0 anywhere — or does the version spec admit 1.107.0 (unpinned, >= , ~= , ^ )? - What did the lockfiles actually resolve to? - Do any Dockerfiles or compose files reference the compromised tags ( v1.107.0 , latest , main-latest ) or the published bad image digest? - Is there a litellm-1.107.0.dist-info in any virtualenv on the box? - Are the implant marker files there — cook.pth , cook.py , remote_code_loader.lock ? Doing that by hand across a few projects and a folder of virtualenvs is exactly the kind of boring, error-prone pass a small tool should do. So I built one. ## litellm-check bash pip install litellm-check litellm-check scan ~/src/my-service Zero third-party dependencies, Python 3.11+. It reads files and package metadata only — it never executes Python (or pip) inside a scanned environment, which is the whole point: the check itself must be safe to run on a suspect machine, ideally with a clean interpreter. A few design choices worth noting: Specs are evaluated, not grepped. A pin of exactly 1.107.0 is critical. A spec that admits it is high — exposure surface, not proof of installation, because whether it actually resolved to 1.107.0 depends on installs inside the announced windows (PyPI 11:39:51–13:23 UTC on Oct 21; Docker Hub until 14:20 UTC; GHCR until 13:51 UTC). A spec that excludes it is reported as info, so a reviewer can see the coverage instead of a silent pass. Every rule traces to the announcement. The 13 rules (LL-001–LL-013) are derived solely from LiteLLM's official incident post — no third-party IOC lists. Each finding in the report carries the file:line evidence, the incident basis, and the remediation (delete the implant files from the shell, kill the daemon holding the lock file, rebuild pinned to litellm==1.106.2 , rotate reachable secrets, check CloudTrail). The limits are printed on every report. A clean scan means "none of the known indicators were found in this tree" — nothing more. Environments rebuilt after exposure, images pulled without any definition file, installs recorded only in CI logs: none of that leaves anything for a file scanner to find. The tool collects evidence; it does not certify anything. The repo ships a deliberately exposed demo project; scanning it produces 16 findings (10 critical, 4 high, 2 info) so you can see the report shape before pointing it at anything real: https://github.com/dylanXM/litellm-check ## The sibling tool: DeepSeek Exposure Scan Same rules-as-data engine shape, different problem. DHS Exclusion and Removal Order #2026-01 (published in the Federal Register on Oct 20) directs federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products — including third-party products built using DeepSeek implementations — and FAR 52.204-30 flows that down to contractors, who now get asked by customers: what model components are inside what you ship? deepseek-scan ( https://github.com/dylanXM/deepseek-scanner ) does the first evidence pass for that question: hosted API endpoints, SDK imports, model ids, dependency manifests and lockfiles, container model pulls, and local weight files — written up as a Markdown or AI-BOM-style JSON report, with the same honesty about what it cannot detect (a renamed, distilled model leaves no textual trace). bash pip install deepseek-scanner Both tools were recently reviewed and merged into the awesome-ai-security-tools list (in its watchlist section — they're new, and the maintainer is right that adoption signals come first). If you try either one, the feedback I value most is false positives and missing rules: both rule sets are single JSON files, so a new detection is a data change, not a code change. Disclosure: I'm the author of both tools. They're Apache-2.0 and not affiliated with BerriAI/LiteLLM or DeepSeek.

title: Maximum Drawdown in Python: Calculate Loss and Recovery Time
author: Alper San
summary: A backtest finishes 26% ahead. In the middle, its value falls from 120 to 90. The final return looks comfortable; the path includes a 25% loss from a previous high. Maximum drawdown is the largest percentage decline from an earlier peak to a later trough within the data you measure. In Python, a running maximum gets you most of the way there. A useful report also needs the peak date, trough date and recovery status. This guide calculates maximum drawdown with pandas, handles an unrecovered loss, and plots an underwater chart. You can run the worked example without an API key, then use the same calculation with a historical market data CSV. Maximum drawdown formula For each observation, keep the highest value seen so far: running peak[t] = maximum value from the start through t drawdown[t] = value[t] / running peak[t] - 1 maximum drawdown = -minimum(drawdown) The drawdown series is zero at a running high and negative below it. We report maximum drawdown as a positive loss magnitude: a drawdown of -0.25 becomes a maximum drawdown of 25% . Other software may return a negative number, so check the convention before combining reports. Order matters. Comparing the highest and lowest values anywhere in a file can put the low before the high. A drawdown requires the peak to happen first. A running maximum preserves that order. A worked example: loss and recovery are different measurements These are illustrative values, not historical prices for a stock or fund. Date in 2026 Value Running peak Drawdown October 1 100 100 0% October 2 120 120 0% October 5 90 120 -25% October 6 108 120 -10% October 7 120 120 0% October 8 126 126 0% The largest decline runs from 120 on October 2 to 90 on October 5. The series regains that peak on October 7. Its final value of 126 is 26% above its starting value, but that return does not describe the loss along the way. The full peak-to-recovery period lasts five calendar days . There are three observation intervals between those dates. Calling both numbers “days underwater” would give the same event two different durations. Calculate maximum drawdown in Python with pandas Install pandas in your project environment: python -m pip install pandas The function below accepts one positive value series with a unique, chronological DatetimeIndex . It rejects missing or invalid observations instead of quietly filling them. That matters because pandas' cummax() normally skips missing values. import math import pandas as pd def drawdown_report ( values ): """ Report the first deepest episode in one positive, dated value series. """ if not isinstance ( values . index , pd . DatetimeIndex ): raise ValueError ( " Use a DatetimeIndex. " ) if values . index . hasnans or not values . index . is_unique : raise ValueError ( " Timestamps must be valid and unique. " ) if not values . index . is_monotonic_increasing : raise ValueError ( " Put observations in chronological order. " ) values = pd . to_numeric ( values , errors = " raise " ). astype ( float ) if len ( values ) < 2 or not values . map ( math . isfinite ). all (): raise ValueError ( " Provide at least two finite observations. " ) if ( values <= 0 ). any (): raise ValueError ( " This calculation requires positive values. " ) running_peak = values . cummax () drawdown = values / running_peak - 1.0 report = { " maximum_drawdown_pct " : - 100 * float ( drawdown . min ()), " current_drawdown_pct " : 100 * float ( drawdown . iloc [ - 1 ]), " peak " : None , " trough " : None , " recovery " : None , " peak_to_trough " : None , " trough_to_recovery " : None , " peak_to_recovery " : None , " elapsed_since_peak_at_end " : None , " peak_to_recovery_intervals " : None , } if drawdown . min () == 0 : return report , drawdown trough = drawdown . idxmin () # First trough when depths tie. peak_value = running_peak . loc [ trough ] before = values . loc [: trough ] peak = before [ before == peak_value ]. index [ - 1 ] after = values . iloc [ values . index . get_loc ( trough ) + 1 :] recovered = after [ after >= peak_value ] recovery = recovered . index [ 0 ] if not recovered . empty else None report . update ( peak = peak , trough = trough , recovery = recovery ) report [ " peak_to_trough " ] = trough - peak if recovery is None : report [ " elapsed_since_peak_at_end " ] = values . index [ - 1 ] - peak else : report [ " trough_to_recovery " ] = recovery - trough report [ " peak_to_recovery " ] = recovery - peak report [ " peak_to_recovery_intervals " ] = ( values . index . get_loc ( recovery ) - values . index . get_loc ( peak ) ) return report , drawdown Run the example: values = pd . Series ( [ 100 , 120 , 90 , 108 , 120 , 126 ], index = pd . to_datetime ([ " 2026-10-01 " , " 2026-10-02 " , " 2026-10-05 " , " 2026-10-06 " , " 2026-10-07 " , " 2026-10-08 " , ], utc = True ), ) report , drawdown = drawdown_report ( values ) print ( f " Maximum drawdown: { report [ ' maximum_drawdown_pct ' ] : . 2 f } % " ) print ( " Peak: " , report [ " peak " ]. date ()) print ( " Trough: " , report [ " trough " ]. date ()) print ( " Recovery: " , report [ " recovery " ]. date ()) print ( " Peak to recovery: " , report [ " peak_to_recovery " ]) The result is a 25.00% maximum drawdown , with an October 2 peak, October 5 trough and October 7 recovery. The final line prints 5 days 00:00:00 . The function uses the first deepest trough when several observations tie. This follows pandas' idxmin() behavior. It then uses the last occurrence of the relevant peak before that trough . If the series reaches 120 twice before falling, the later 120 is the start of that loss episode. Recovery is the first later observation that meets or exceeds the old peak. Those conventions make the dates reproducible. They do not claim to identify the longest underwater episode, which may be a different event from the deepest loss. Report an unrecovered drawdown without inventing a date Stop the example at 108, before the series regains 120: unfinished = values . iloc [: 4 ] open_report , _ = drawdown_report ( unfinished ) print ( open_report [ " maximum_drawdown_pct " ]) # 25.0 print ( round ( open_report [ " current_drawdown_pct " ], 2 )) # -10.0 print ( open_report [ " recovery " ]) # None print ( open_report [ " elapsed_since_peak_at_end " ]) # 4 days The worst observed decline is still 25%. At the end of this shorter file, the value is 10% below its peak. Recovery is unobserved within this dataset . It is not zero days, and the calculation cannot supply a future recovery date. A report card can say: Field Result for the shortened example Maximum drawdown 25.00% Current drawdown -10.00% Peak date October 2, 2026 Trough date October 5, 2026 Recovery Not recovered by the final observation Elapsed since peak at the end 4 calendar days If the worst episode recovered but the series later fell again, the current drawdown describes that later decline. It should not inherit the earlier episode's recovery date. Keep “maximum drawdown” and “current drawdown” as separate fields. Use historical stock data from a CSV export For an AAPL analysis, use a historical CSV with one observation per daily bar. Save your input as aapl-daily.csv . Verify the date range, currency and adjustment policy before calculating the result. This example expects Time (UTC) and Close column headers. Rename your own columns explicitly if their names differ: frame = pd . read_csv ( " aapl-daily.csv " ) prices = pd . Series ( pd . to_numeric ( frame [ " Close " ], errors = " raise " ). to_numpy (), index = pd . to_datetime ( frame [ " Time (UTC) " ], utc = True , errors = " raise " ), name = " AAPL close " , ) stock_report , stock_drawdown = drawdown_report ( prices ) print ( f " Maximum drawdown: { stock_report [ ' maximum_drawdown_pct ' ] : . 2 f } % " ) print ( " Recovery: " , stock_report [ " recovery " ]) The CSV supplies prices; the script calculates the statistic locally. It makes no extra API requests. Keep the symbol, date range, bar interval, quote currency and price basis alongside the result, since those choices are not all encoded in the price column itself. For a portfolio or strategy, supply a suitable equity or cumulative wealth series instead. Deposits and withdrawals can move an account balance without representing investment performance. A cash-flow-adjusted performance series avoids treating a deposit as a gain or a withdrawal as a market loss. Plot an underwater chart An underwater chart shows the distance below the running peak. Its zero line means the series is at a high within the selected window. A deeper negative value means a larger decline from that high. python -m pip install matplotlib import matplotlib.pyplot as plt ax = ( 100 * drawdown ). plot ( figsize = ( 9 , 3 ), color = " #9c3948 " ) ax . fill_between ( drawdown . index , 100 * drawdown , 0 , color = " #9c3948 " , alpha = 0.15 ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = " gray " , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set ( title = " Drawdown from the running peak " , ylabel = " Drawdown (%) " ) ax . set_xlabel ( " Observation timestamp (UTC) " ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Replace drawdown with stock_drawdown to plot the CSV result. Avoid presenting the illustrative series as an asset's actual performance. Why two maximum drawdown results can disagree The formula is short. The data choices around it deserve just as much attention. Choice What it changes Analysis window An earlier peak outside the file is invisible to the calculation. Daily closes versus intraday observations Daily closes can miss a deeper loss inside a session. Price series versus total-return series Distributions and corporate-action treatment affect the path. Missing or duplicate observations A missing trough or repeated timestamp can distort the result. Portfolio cash flows Raw balances can mix external transfers with investment performance. A one-year maximum drawdown is measured within that year. If you need a peak from before the reporting start date, include the earlier data and state how you separate the peak-estimation period from the reporting period. Do not label a short sample as an all-time drawdown. Daily OHLCV closes produce a closing-observation drawdown. They do not recover the sequence of every high and low inside each candle. Comparing every bar's high to its low can also assume an order that OHLC data does not reveal. Our guide to ambiguous OHLC backtests explains that limitation. State the adjustment policy. Unadjusted stock prices, split-adjusted prices and a total-return series answer different questions. The adjusted versus unadjusted prices guide covers the difference. This Python function does not adjust prices or reinvest distributions for you. Keep timestamps honest. Bar timestamps may label the start of a period rather than the instant of the closing trade. Retain the provider's convention when naming peak and trough observations. Count calendar duration from timestamps and observation intervals from positions; do not silently substitute one for the other. How much gain is needed to recover a drawdown? A 25% loss requires a 33.33% gain from the trough to regain the old peak. The gain is measured from the smaller value: required recovery gain = 1 / (1 - loss fraction) - 1 Loss from the peak Gain needed from the trough 10% 11.11% 20% 25.00% 25% 33.33% 50% 100.00% This is arithmetic, not a forecast of when recovery will happen. Maximum drawdown describes the path in the observed sample; it does not cap a future loss. A useful drawdown report includes the data window, observation frequency, price basis, deepest episode dates and whether recovery was observed. Keep those assumptions beside the percentage.

title: How I Fixed TTS Hallucinations Without Regenerating Everything
author: Julian Brown
summary: The audit had done its job. I knew where the generated audiobook didn’t match the manuscript. Now I had another problem. Most of the audio around those errors was already good. The pacing worked. The voices worked. The performances worked. Regenerating an entire chapter to fix one localized problem meant asking the TTS model to recreate all of that again. And generative audio isn’t deterministic in the ways that matter here. A new generation could change the pacing, emphasis, pauses, emotional delivery, or interaction between voices. I might fix one sentence and lose a performance I already liked. So I stopped thinking about the chapter as something that needed to be regenerated. I started treating it like recorded audio that needed a punch-in. Borrowing From the Recording Studio A punch-in is a familiar idea in audio production. If a musician makes a mistake in one section of an otherwise good recording, you don’t necessarily record the entire performance again. You replace the bad section. The same idea works surprisingly well with generated narration. Instead of: Bad section ↓ Regenerate entire chapter ↓ Hope the new performance is as good I wanted: Good audio ↓ Identify corrupted region ↓ Generate replacement ↓ Match replacement to existing audio ↓ Splice it in ↓ Keep everything else The idea was simple. Making the replacement disappear into the existing performance required three things. Patch Contextual Units, Not Isolated Errors If one word is wrong, generating only that word sounds like the obvious solution. But speech doesn’t work as isolated tokens. Delivery depends on what surrounds a word: pacing, sentence rhythm, emphasis, pauses, and emotional context. So the unit of repair shouldn’t necessarily be the unit of error. If one word is wrong, I may regenerate the sentence. If a sentence is corrupted, I may regenerate the surrounding exchange. The goal is to give the model enough context for a natural performance without replacing more good audio than necessary. Keep the Repair Verbatim The Chapter 9 failure had already demonstrated what could happen when a generative TTS model wandered beyond the manuscript. A repair pass isn’t the place to invite more creativity. The model’s job isn’t to improve or continue the passage. It’s to perform the supplied text verbatim. Conceptually: Speak the supplied text exactly as written. Do not add dialogue. Do not omit dialogue. Do not paraphrase. Do not continue beyond the supplied text. The creative freedom I wanted was in the performance, not the words. Match the Existing Master Even a good replacement can sound like a patch if it doesn’t match the audio around it. So before inserting the replacement, I ran it through the same mastering process as the original chapter. The goal was simple: when the replacement enters, it shouldn’t announce itself as replacement audio. With those three constraints in place, I could repair the actual failure. Repairing the 73-Second Hallucination Chapter 9 was the obvious test. The TTS model had invented roughly 73 seconds of dialogue that wasn’t in the manuscript before eventually finding its way back to the real script. I didn’t want to regenerate the chapter. I wanted to remove the corrupted region and replace it with the exchange that should have been there. The repair region ran from approximately 03:46 to 05:06.75 . That range is wider than the 73-second hallucination itself because the edit needs usable boundaries around the corrupted material rather than cutting at the exact instant the model begins and ends its tangent. The repair became three pieces: Original audio before corruption + Newly generated replacement + Original audio after corruption Using FFmpeg, the operation looked conceptually like this: ffmpeg \ -i chapter_09_master.wav \ -i chapter_09_patch.wav \ -filter_complex " [0:a]atrim=start=0:end=226,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[before]; [1:a]asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[patch]; [0:a]atrim=start=306.75,asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[after]; [before][patch][after]concat=n=3:v=0:a=1[out] " \ -map "[out]" \ chapter_09_repaired.wav The original chapter stays intact before the edit. The hallucinated region disappears. The newly generated exchange takes its place. Then the original performance resumes. The Result The repaired Chapter 9 dropped from roughly 11 minutes to about 9:51 . The difference wasn’t compression. It was more than a minute of generated material that never belonged there. The intended exchange was restored, and the rest of the performance stayed intact. That was the important part. I didn’t need the model to recreate a chapter that was mostly good. I only needed it to recreate the part that failed. Fix what failed. Keep what worked.

title: Starting a Local Directory From Public Records: Notes on the License Frame
author: Nearbia
summary: Most local business directories begin with whatever businesses submit about themselves. We are trying the opposite order for Nearbia : start with the records that say who is allowed to do the work, then find websites, then check each site. The directory is not live yet. What is live is a set of plain guides and a work log, and this post walks through the data side of that work. Why start with licenses In Florida, contracting without a state license is a crime, and the state's Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) is the body that issues trade licenses. For a directory of contractors, that makes the license file a natural "frame": the set of entities that should be in scope before you look at anything else. The license data itself is surprisingly structured. A Florida contractor license number starts with a few letters, and those letters encode two things: The trade. CFC is a certified plumbing contractor, CAC is air conditioning, CGC is general, EC is electrical. Two easy ones to misread: CCC is roofing and CPC is pool/spa. The scope. Codes starting with C are certified (passed a board-approved exam, valid in any Florida jurisdiction). Codes starting with R are registered (met local competency rules, valid only where those rules were met). If you are modelling this, the prefix is effectively a compound key: trade + scope . Treat "certified vs registered" as a first-class field, because it changes where a business can legally work. The stages, as a pipeline The Nearbia work log lays the process out in stages. Paraphrased as a pipeline: National list of websites. Free open datasets of US places are downloaded whole. Each website gets one key so duplicates collapse. License frame. Florida's contractor license file lists everyone allowed to work. The log notes the state site blocks automated downloads, so a saved copy from a public web archive is used, and freshness is not guaranteed. That is an honest constraint worth designing around: version your snapshots and record their dates. City domain list. Sites with a plumbing category or name, inside or near city limits, are pulled from the national list. Other candidate sources. Building permits, the state business entity registry, and paid search listings for the city. Merge into companies. Records join on license number, then phone, then name and city, then final domain after redirects. Place addresses in city limits. A mailing city is not a city boundary. Website check in a real browser. The first slice is deliberately small: one trade (plumbers) in one city (St. Petersburg, Florida). Things that bite you Join order matters. License number is the strongest key when present. Phone numbers are shared, recycled and tracked. Names drift ("Inc." vs "LLC", DBAs). Domains redirect. Ordering joins from strongest to weakest key keeps bad matches from cascading. Mailing city ≠ city. The work log points out that some St. Petersburg ZIP codes reach into Seminole, Kenneth City and Pinellas Park. If your city page filters on the mailing city string, you will list businesses that are not in the city. Geocode and test against the actual boundary. Neighbouring cities overlap. The log reports that St. Petersburg and Clearwater shared about 80% of the same companies within a radius in their tests. Their decision: a city page lists only companies with an office inside that city. Whatever you choose, make the rule explicit, because "serves the area" and "is located here" are different claims. Not every record says what you think. A local business tax receipt is not a contractor license. Registering an LLC does not qualify anyone to contract. If you are merging state corporate filings with license data, keep them as separate attributes rather than collapsing them into one "verified" flag. Public records are a toolbox Beyond licenses, Florida law opens state, county and city records to inspection by anyone, with specific exceptions. For a contractor, that includes corporate filings and fictitious names (Sunbiz), building permits (county portals), code enforcement cases, court dockets and liens, OSHA inspections, and federal exclusions in SAM.gov. Each answers a different question, and each has blind spots. A permit portal, for example, cannot show work that was done without a permit. Where to read more The full write-ups, including the stage table with dates and the record-by-record reference, are in the work log published by Nearbia . If you work with licensing or permit data and have hit any of the same problems, I would be glad to hear how you handled them in the comments.

title: One Skill, Many Career Opportunities: Why Digital Marketing Is the Future
author: Priarya
summary: * What if one skill could open the door to multiple career opportunities? * From helping brands grow online to building your own business, digital marketing offers exciting possibilities. As more businesses move online, the need for people with digital marketing skills is creating new opportunities. Whether you're a student, fresher, job seeker, or aspiring entrepreneur, learning digital marketing can help you explore different career paths. Why Is Digital Marketing Becoming So Important? Think about how you discover a new product, find a salon, or search for a course. You probably use Google, Instagram, or another online platform. Businesses want to reach customers wherever they spend time online. Digital marketing helps them build visibility, connect with the right audience, generate enquiries, and promote their services. From small local businesses to large companies, organisations use digital platforms to grow their brands. As online habits continue to change, digital marketing skills can help learners prepare for opportunities across different industries. What Exactly Is Digital Marketing? Digital marketing means promoting products, services, or brands through online platforms such as search engines, websites, social media, and email. But it is much more than posting pictures or running advertisements. It involves understanding customers, creating useful content, choosing suitable marketing channels, and measuring results. For example, a student searching for a digital marketing course in Varanasi might discover an institute through Google, visit its website, and check its social media before enquiring. Different digital marketing strategies help businesses connect with potential customers throughout this journey. Explore the Skills That Make Digital Marketing Powerful Digital marketing includes several specialisations. You can explore different areas and choose the ones that match your interests. Search Engine Optimization (SEO) SEO helps websites improve their visibility in organic search results. It includes keyword research, on-page optimization, technical SEO, content improvement, and link building. If you enjoy research, website analysis, and problem-solving, SEO could be an interesting starting point. Social Media Marketing Social media marketing helps businesses connect with audiences through platforms such as Instagram, Facebook, and LinkedIn. It involves content planning, creative posts, audience engagement, and performance tracking. This field can suit people who enjoy creativity and communication. Content Marketing Content marketing focuses on creating useful blogs, articles, website pages, and other material that answers audience questions. If you enjoy writing and explaining ideas, content marketing can be a valuable skill to develop. Paid Advertising Businesses use platforms such as Google Ads to promote products and services to selected audiences. This field involves campaign planning, budgeting, targeting, and analysing results. It can suit people who enjoy strategy and working with data. Website Analytics Tools such as Google Analytics 4 (GA4) and Google Search Console help marketers understand website activity and search performance. Analytics helps you identify what is working, understand audience behaviour, and make better-informed marketing decisions. How to Start Learning Digital Marketing Step by Step You do not need to learn everything at once. Start with the basics and build your skills gradually. Step 1: Understand the fundamentals. Learn how businesses attract customers online and how different digital marketing channels work together. Step 2: Explore different skills. Understand the basics of SEO, social media marketing, content creation, paid advertising, and analytics. Step 3: Learn relevant tools. Practise using tools such as Google Search Console, Google Analytics 4, and Google Keyword Planner. Step 4: Work on practical projects. Research keywords, write an SEO-friendly article, create a social media calendar, or analyse a website. Step 5: Choose your specialisation. Focus on the area you enjoy most and develop deeper knowledge through regular practice. Step 6: Build your portfolio. Collect your projects and work samples to demonstrate your skills when applying for jobs, internships, or freelance projects. Following these steps can help you move from basic knowledge towards practical experience. Career Opportunities After Learning Digital Marketing One of the biggest advantages of digital marketing is the variety of career paths you can explore. SEO Executive: Improves website visibility in search engines. Social Media Executive: Plans content and manages social media activities. Digital Marketing Executive: Supports different online marketing campaigns. Content Writer: Creates blogs, articles, and website content. PPC Executive: Helps manage paid advertising campaigns. Digital Marketing Analyst: Studies marketing data and campaign performance. Freelancer: Provides digital marketing services to clients. You can also use these skills to promote your own business or build a personal brand. The opportunities available to you depend on your practical knowledge, portfolio, communication skills, and experience. Can You Build a Career by Starting with Just One Skill? Yes! You can start with one skill and expand your knowledge as you grow. For example, you can begin with SEO by learning keyword research, on-page optimization, and basic website audits. After practising these skills, you can build a portfolio and apply for internships or entry-level positions. Similarly, someone interested in writing can start with content creation and gradually learn SEO-friendly writing and content strategy. As your experience grows, you can add related skills. An SEO professional might learn analytics, while a social media executive might explore paid advertising. One skill can be your starting point, while continuous learning can help you explore more opportunities. Job, Freelancing, or Your Own Business? Digital marketing can support different professional goals. Build a career: Start with internships or entry-level positions to gain experience and learn professional workflows. Become a freelancer: Offer services such as SEO, content writing, or social media management to clients. Start your own business: Use digital marketing to promote your products, reach customers, and build an online presence. Build a personal brand: Share useful content and demonstrate your knowledge to develop a professional identity. Each path requires dedication, continuous learning, and the ability to deliver results. There is no guaranteed shortcut to success, but practical skills can help you explore different options. How to Choose the Right Digital Marketing Course in Varanasi A structured learning programme can help you understand digital marketing concepts and practise them in the right order. Before enrolling, check the syllabus, practical assignments, project opportunities, trainer support, and tools covered. Also understand the course fees, certification details, and placement assistance offered. If you are looking for a digital marketing course in Varanasi, you can explore DIDM Varanasi and review its available course details to see whether the programme matches your goals. Remember, a course can provide direction, but your progress also depends on regular practice, curiosity, and your willingness to improve. Start Building Your Future with Digital Marketing Digital marketing brings together creativity, technology, communication, and business strategy. It allows you to explore different specialisations and apply your skills across industries. You can start with one skill, gain practical experience, build a portfolio, and gradually expand your expertise. Your career does not have to start with knowing everything. It can start with learning one useful skill and taking the next step.

title: Building a Client-Side QR Code Debugger with 6 Optical Tests and 10 Languages
author: RahaLune QR Studio
summary: Have you ever scanned a QR code that looked perfectly fine on a high-resolution screen, but failed miserably when printed? It happens all the time. Low contrast, missing quiet zones, or oversized logos can easily break the error correction data inside a QR code, rendering it useless to smartphone cameras. To solve this, we built the RahaLune QR Code Debugger. It is a 100% client-side tool that runs six standardized optical tests on any uploaded QR code image, giving users a clear scannability score before they send anything to the printer. Recently, we rolled out a massive update: native translation into 10 languages, including full Right-to-Left layout support for Arabic and Urdu. Here is a look at how we built it and the technical challenges we solved along the way. The 6 Optical Tests When a user uploads an image, the tool processes it locally and runs the following checks: ** WCAG 2.1 Luminance:** Calculates the contrast ratio between the foreground modules and the background. If it falls below the 4.5 to 1 accessibility threshold, it flags a warning. Quiet Zone (Margin): Verifies that there is enough uninterrupted white space around the perimeter, at least 4 modules, for scanners to detect the code boundaries. Print Quality: Evaluates pixel dimensions against standard 300 DPI print requirements to prevent blurry outputs. Error Recovery: Identifies the Reed-Solomon resilience level to determine how much damage the code can sustain. Logo Impact: Measures center obstruction to ensure brand logos do not exceed the 30% error correction ceiling. Native Scan Test: Runs parallel decode trials using both the jsQR library and the native BarcodeDetector API to simulate real-world hardware and mobile scanners. The Localization Challenge We wanted the tool to be accessible globally, so we translated the entire interface into 10 languages: English, French, Spanish, German, Turkish, Chinese, Indonesian, Malay, Arabic, and Urdu. Since RahaLune is a purely client-side React application, we opted for a lightweight JSON-based translation strategy. We dynamically load the correct JSON file based on the URL parameter. This keeps the initial JavaScript bundle size small and ensures fast load times. Handling Right-to-Left Layouts Supporting Arabic and Urdu was not just about swapping text strings. It required a complete structural layout flip. If you are building a web app with Right-to-Left support, avoid hardcoding directional styles like margin-left or padding-right. Instead, embrace CSS logical properties. For example, use margin-inline-start instead of margin-left, and padding-inline-end instead of padding-right. We also dynamically update the root HTML element based on the user's selected language, setting the direction attribute to Right-to-Left or Left-to-Right accordingly. This ensures that the six inspection cards, navigation menus, and drag-and-drop upload zones mirror perfectly for Right-to-Left languages, while native font rendering keeps the typography feeling natural. SEO for Localized Client-Side Apps Making the app multilingual is only half the battle. Ensuring it gets found is the other half. To ensure the localized pages rank well, we dynamically update the page title, meta description, and Open Graph tags based on the active language. Additionally, we programmatically inject hreflang tags into the page head to tell search engines exactly where the different language versions are hosted, preventing duplicate content issues and boosting regional search visibility. Try It Out We now have a QR code debugger that speaks 10 languages, processes data entirely in the browser, and remains 100% free forever. No logins, no ads, and no server-side image tracking. If you want to see how the Right-to-Left layout handles the six inspection cards, switch the language to Arabic or Urdu using the header dropdown. Try the Multi-Language QR Code Debugger here: https://rahalune-qr-studio.vercel.app/debugger

title: Grounded answers: how Graphify tags what it knows
author: Syed Fahad
summary: Confidence tags on a Graphify graph say how each edge was established, before an agent follows it. EXTRACTED means tree-sitter found the call, import, or definition in the syntax tree. INFERRED means a model connected it. AMBIGUOUS means the evidence did not resolve, and the edge stays flagged. Read the tag before you trust the hop. What do the confidence tags mean? A code knowledge graph stores functions, classes, and docs as nodes. Calls, imports, and references are the edges between them. The edge is the claim the assistant walks. Confidence tags are the label on that claim. How Graphify works builds the graph in two stages, and the tag says which stage produced the edge. EXTRACTED comes from the syntax tree. Graphify parses code on the machine with tree-sitter. The parser finds the call, the import, or the definition, and that edge is deterministic. Parse the same file again and the parser finds the same edge. No model sits in that step. The Cursor integration describes this tag as parsed from the AST. INFERRED is a connection a model made. Docs, PDFs, SQL schemas, and Terraform are not a tree of calls. The model you configure joins a doc page to the service it describes, or a Terraform resource to the code that uses it. Those edges are usually right. They are still a judgment, and the tag says so. A plausible link can be wrong. The tag is how you see that the link was proposed. AMBIGUOUS means Graphify found evidence and could not resolve it. The cases named in the glossary are dynamic dispatch, reflection, and an import built from a string. The edge stays in the graph with the flag, so the unresolved link is visible as unresolved. graphify explain shows how each connection on a node was established. GRAPH_REPORT.md separates the architecture the parser extracted from the connections the model proposed. Over MCP, graph_stats and the confidence audit in the report break the graph down by the three tags, so you can see how much of the map is parsed fact. Why should an agent read the tag before the next hop? An answer from the graph is a path. Each hop names a file and a line, and the edge on that hop carries one tag. The tags are different evidence. A caller the parser found and a doc the model attached can both appear in the same path, and the output keeps them distinct. Treat every hop as fact and an INFERRED link gets the same weight as an EXTRACTED call. That is how a guessed connection becomes an edit. The glossary uses this picture: the payment worker depends on the sessions table. You want to see whether the parser found that, or a model inferred it, before you change the code. Lean on an EXTRACTED hop when you change code. Treat an INFERRED hop as a lead, and open the doc and the symbol. Treat an AMBIGUOUS hop as a place to read the source, because the evidence stopped short of a resolved link. A similarity score says two chunks resemble each other. It does not record whether a relationship was parsed or proposed. That difference is the subject of Code knowledge graph vs RAG . Where do confidence tags not help? The tag describes an edge. It does not answer "find this string." Grep returns the lines that contain the string. A misspelled word in a comment, or a URL in a config file, is that question. Grep answers the hop you can phrase as a string. A tag will not. Fuzzy search over a large body of prose is the other miss. Embeddings are the better tool there, and Graphify does not try to beat them. A tag will not find the paragraph that only resembles the question. What runs on the machine? The open-source engine is Apache 2.0. Code parsing happens on your machine. There is no telemetry. INFERRED edges use the model backend you configure, and that backend can be a local one, so the judgment can stay on the machine too. The graph is files in graphify-out/ : graph.html , GRAPH_REPORT.md , and graph.json . Graphify Cloud hosts the same kind of graph and keeps it current. It is a different product. uv tool install graphifyy The package on PyPI is graphifyy (two y's). pipx install graphifyy also works. Then graphify install , and in the assistant /graphify . . The command reference is in the docs .

title: Oracle put ChatGPT inside finance workflows. The user count is not the story.
author: VOXA
summary: Oracle and OpenAI expanded their partnership on 27 October, and the announcement contained two numbers that people will quote for different reasons. The first is 130,000 active ChatGPT users inside Oracle. The second is 95,000 active Codex users. Both are large. Neither tells you whether the work changed. What Oracle actually shipped Three pieces, and only one of them is about chat. Oracle AI Workspace, still in development, is meant to let a person describe a task and have it completed across Oracle's finance, procurement and planning applications, inside the organisation's permissions and approvals. That is the interesting part: the assistant becomes a front door to systems that already hold the money. Second, Oracle is putting OpenAI models inside its own products, including a small business bundle that pairs ChatGPT Business and Codex with Oracle applications and cloud credits. Third, procurement. US customers can buy API access, Codex and ChatGPT Work through Oracle Marketplace, using existing contracts and eligible Oracle credits. That is a distribution move, and it is how a lot of enterprise AI will actually be bought: on the contract that already exists, not on a new one. The chip line is the real signal Buried under the assistant news: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure will add Google TPUs, OpenAI's new accelerator and Cerebras hardware alongside its existing options. A database company adding three non-Nvidia accelerators in one announcement is a supply decision. It says the constraint on AI capacity is still silicon, and that buyers will spread across vendors to get it. If you are budgeting for inference next year, that is more useful than any user count. Why 130,000 users is weak evidence An active user number tells you adoption, and adoption is the cheapest thing to buy. Hand out licences, wait a month, count logins. It says nothing about output, and it is not comparable across companies because "active" is defined by whoever is reporting. It is also the number that appears in press releases, which is exactly why it deserves a second look. The number that is actually useful In the same announcement, Oracle mentioned its recruiting team uses ChatGPT Work for market research that used to take two to four days, and now takes 15 to 20 minutes to prepare. That is one task, one team, with a before and an after. It is still preparation time rather than total cycle time, so the end-to-end gain is smaller than the headline suggests, but it is measurable, and that is the difference. If you are evaluating a rollout inside your own company, that is the format to demand: one process, one baseline, one new number, one date. What this looks like when it fails Apollo's chief economist made the macro version of the same point this week: margins are rising for the largest technology companies and flat across the rest of the S&P 500. Adoption is high. The productivity number is not moving yet. The gap is not mysterious. Tools get added on top of an unchanged process, the process keeps its bottleneck, and the dashboard shows usage instead of output. The governance question nobody asked If an agent is acting inside finance and procurement, the questions are the ones that keep coming up in every serious deployment: what scope does it hold, where is the approval gate, what does the log record, and how fast can you revoke it. An agent that can read a purchase order and draft one is useful. An agent that can approve one is a governance decision wearing a product name. Oracle's own framing, about access governed by each organisation's permissions and approvals, is the whole pitch and the whole risk at once. There is a practical checklist for this in the guide we published today at voxahq.in/guides/ai-agent-erp-access: read, draft and submit scopes, never approve, a spend ceiling per run, an approval gate before anything leaves the company, and a log the agent cannot edit. Two questions for your own team Which task has a before and after we can name? And which number moved: cycle time, cost per case, revenue per person, or hours per week? If nobody can answer both in one sentence, the rollout is a subscription with a dashboard. That is fine as a starting point, but it is not evidence, and it should not justify the next licence increase. What this means if you are a 20-person company Very little, directly, and that is worth saying. Oracle AI Workspace is aimed at organisations that already run Oracle finance and procurement. If you do not, the announcement is a signal rather than a product. The signal is that the assistant is moving inside the system of record. That changes the evaluation question for everyone else. Instead of asking which chatbot writes better copy, the question becomes which of your existing tools can hand an agent a narrow, auditable permission to do one job. Most mid-size stacks already can. The constraint is usually nobody has written down which job, which scope and which number proves it worked. The procurement shift is the part to copy Buying AI through a marketplace, using credits you already committed, removes a procurement cycle that can take a quarter. That is why announcements like this move faster inside large companies than any pilot programme. For a small team the equivalent is simpler: put AI spend on the card that already exists, cap it monthly, and require one number per tool before renewal. The discipline does the same job as the marketplace. Originally published at voxahq.in . Sources: OpenAI and Oracle announcement, 27 October 2026; Apollo note on AI payoff, 24 October 2026.

title: Why graphs beat vectors for agent memory
author: Syed Fahad
summary: A code graph stores the calls and imports in a codebase, and the assistant still has them next session. A vector database stores text that resembles the question, then searches again. The code graph vs vector database difference is what the assistant remembers. How does a code graph differ from a vector database? A code graph stores typed entities and the relationships between them. A Knowledge graph is that structure. The entities are the things in the repo. The edges are how they connect, and an assistant can traverse them. A vector database stores embeddings and metadata filters. A filter limits which vectors return. The relationship lives on the graph as an edge, and that edge is still there when the assistant starts again. How similarity and structure compare as ways to fetch an answer is in Code knowledge graph vs RAG . What does a query return? A graph query is a typed, multi-hop traversal. The assistant follows edges of a given type, one hop after another. A vector query is approximate nearest-neighbour search, a top-k of the chunks whose embeddings sit nearest the question. Graphify vs vector databases sets the two side by side. Pinecone, Weaviate, and pgvector return the most similar vectors. The graph returns the entities and the relationships between them. For an assistant, that result is the memory. What happens on the second hop? The gap shows up when a question has two steps. A top-k lookup is one round of nearest-neighbour search, so a second hop needs the first answer before it can even be phrased. The model is left stitching disconnected chunks together. On a graph the second hop is one more edge. A later session follows that same edge, because the edge was stored with the graph. What stays when a file changes? Changing a file means re-embedding and upserting every chunk it touched before any of it can be retrieved again. Graphify re-parses that one file and updates its nodes. The edges that did not change stay. The cost of keeping current is the size of the change, not the size of the repository. Inside the assistant, the command is /graphify . --update . How can you check an answer? A vector result comes with a similarity score. The score measures how near two vectors were. A graph result is the path the answer took. Every edge on that path carries a confidence tag: EXTRACTED, INFERRED, or AMBIGUOUS. The tag is stored on the edge, so the next session can read that path. Where does the text go? Vector data is often shipped to an embedding API. Graphify is on-device, and it sends no telemetry. Where does a vector database still win? Graphify vs vector databases has nine rows. Eight of them are a real difference. The ninth is the one they win. A vector index answers what looks like this, and for fuzzy similarity over large volumes of prose it is still the better tool. Can you run both? You can run both. Some teams keep a vector index for semantic recall and use Graphify for structure. Graphify can store embeddings as node attributes, so similarity stays one signal inside a traversal. Hybrid search blends keyword and vector scores. What comes back is still a ranked list of disconnected chunks. A graph returns connected entities, and the structure survives retrieval. Graphify vs RAG is that choice for a retrieval pipeline. After the session ends, those connections are on the graph. Does Graphify replace Pinecone, Weaviate, or pgvector? As coding-assistant memory, retrieval becomes a traversal over typed edges. The answer arrives as connected entities, and the path is there to read. Graphify does not replace Pinecone, Weaviate, or pgvector for every workload. Those products keep their place for pure similarity, and Graphify runs alongside them. Is Graphify a graph database like Neo4j? Graphify is a memory layer. It builds the graph from your codebase and serves it over MCP and the CLI. There is no schema to model and no queries to write. If you already run Neo4j or FalkorDB, it exports into them. Proof Steve Scargall, at MemVerge, reported 79× fewer tokens on a 496K-token codebase, with no vector database in the stack. That is his measurement, not a Graphify benchmark. Install The package on PyPI is graphifyy . Install the CLI, then register it with your assistant. uv tool install graphifyy graphify install In the project, build the graph. /graphify .

title: How to give GitHub Copilot codebase context that persists
author: Syed Fahad
summary: GitHub Copilot codebase context vanishes when the chat ends, because each session starts from zero and Copilot searches the repo again. A graph built once on your machine is a map Copilot can query the next time. Graphify builds that graph and registers it with Copilot. How do you give GitHub Copilot codebase context? The GitHub Copilot integration page wires this in two commands, then a graph of the repo. The package on PyPI is graphifyy (two y's). uv tool install graphifyy pipx install graphifyy also works. graphify install graphify install registers the /graphify skill and an MCP server, so Copilot can query the graph. Graphify speaks the Model Context Protocol . Any MCP client talks to the same server and the same ten graph tools. The integration page points at the docs for how to point Copilot at that server. Build the graph on the project you have open. In Copilot, run: /graphify . Tree-sitter parses the code locally, so call and import edges come from the syntax tree. Docs and other non-code files are read by the model you already use. The map lands in graphify-out/ as graph.html , GRAPH_REPORT.md , and graph.json . The next session queries those files. The architecture is already on disk. A knowledge graph here means entities and the typed relationships between them. The same shape of setup for Cursor is How to give Cursor a code knowledge graph . What can Copilot ask once the graph exists? The questions on the integration page are the ones that used to mean reading a large slice of the repo. What calls chargeCustomer , and what breaks if the signature changes. The path from a checkout endpoint to the table it writes. Which modules read a config value such as STRIPE_KEY . How the auth subsystem hangs together before you touch it. You can run the same questions from the shell. The page names these commands: graphify query "what calls chargeCustomer" graphify path "checkout" "database" graphify explain "AuthService" graphify prs graphify query returns a scoped piece of the graph. graphify path walks the hops between two nodes. graphify explain lists the edges on one symbol. graphify prs is the pull-request command listed beside them. The docs cover its flags. Every edge Copilot gets back carries a confidence tag. EXTRACTED was parsed from the AST with tree-sitter. INFERRED means a model connected non-code material, such as a doc to the service it describes, and the tag marks that judgment. AMBIGUOUS means there was evidence and it could not be fully resolved, as with dynamic dispatch or an import built from a string. The edge is kept and flagged. When Copilot returns a path, open the file and line on the hop you are about to trust, and read the tag on that edge. An EXTRACTED edge is the parser. An INFERRED edge is the model joining a doc or a schema to code. It can be wrong and still sound plausible. An AMBIGUOUS edge is unresolved evidence, kept so the gap stays visible. The integration page describes the return value as connected structure, a path, which still holds past one or two hops. A pile of matching files, with the links guessed in the chat, is the loop this replaces. What does the graph leave to you? The graph does not update itself. After the code changes, run /graphify . again, or /graphify . --update to re-scan only what changed. From the shell, graphify update . does that pass. graphify hook install adds post-commit and post-checkout git hooks that refresh the changed files. Until you refresh, Copilot is reading the last map you built. Grep still wins when the question is "find this string." The graph is for relationships. A literal string in a comment is still a search. The open-source engine runs on your machine. Code parsing is local. There is no telemetry. Graphify Cloud is the hosted graph. This guide is the on-device setup. Cloud is a different product. How do you confirm it is wired? uv tool install graphifyy graphify install Then, in Copilot: /graphify . The command reference is in the docs . Copilot-specific notes stay on the GitHub Copilot integration page.

title: Best codebase-context tools for AI coding assistants (2026)
author: Syed Fahad
summary: The best codebase context tools depend on the question you are asking. Grep finds a string. Embeddings, RAG, and a vector database find prose that resembles the question. A code knowledge graph follows a relationship you can open. Hosted search and review tools serve a person, or a pull request. Question A tool that fits Find this string grep Prose that resembles the question Embeddings, RAG, or a vector database What calls what, hop by hop A code knowledge graph Search across the organisation Sourcegraph Comments on an open pull request Greptile or CodeRabbit Code that looks like this, inside Cursor Cursor's own index What is grep best at? Grep is best when the question is "find this string." It returns the lines that contain the text. One hop is usually in reach too: the direct callers of a function, when the name in the call matches the name you searched. Past that hop, text search gets worse. A question such as what breaks if this schema changes runs through the table, the queries, the services, and the endpoints. Each hop adds name collisions, re-exports, and files that mention the symbol without touching it. What are embeddings, RAG, and a vector database best at? They are best at fuzzy recall over prose. Graphify vs RAG describes retrieval-augmented generation the way Lewis et al. (2020) introduced it: split documents into chunks, embed them, and pull back the top-k most similar. That works for lookup, when the answer sits in one passage. A relationship is a different shape. Chunking drops the link between a function and its caller. A two-hop question needs the first answer before the second can be asked, which is why benchmarks such as HotpotQA exist. Graphify vs vector databases names Pinecone, Weaviate, and pgvector: nearest-neighbour search returns similar vectors. A metadata filter narrows that search. Hybrid search still comes back as a ranked list of disconnected chunks. A changed file is re-embedded before those chunks can be retrieved again. A similarity score measures resemblance, and you judge the answer yourself. Chunks in a typical embedding pipeline go to an embedding API. Keep the vector index when the corpus is prose. Some teams run both: vectors for semantic recall, a graph for relationships. Graphify can store an embedding as one signal on a node, and retrieval is still a walk. If you already run Neo4j or FalkorDB, the graph exports into them. The essay form of this argument is Code knowledge graph vs RAG . What is a code knowledge graph best at? A code knowledge graph is best when the assistant needs a relationship: what calls this, what a change reaches, the path from one symbol to another. Graphify builds that graph from the repo. Code is parsed on the machine with tree-sitter, and each edge carries a confidence tag: EXTRACTED from the syntax tree, INFERRED by a model, or AMBIGUOUS when the evidence did not resolve. An answer is a path you can open. There is no telemetry on the open-source engine. Graphify Cloud is the hosted graph. It is a different product. Graphify is the wrong tool for two of the jobs in the table. Fuzzy prose still belongs to embeddings. "Find this string" still belongs to grep. What are hosted search and review tools best at? Graphify vs Sourcegraph is a code search platform people use. The index covers the organisation, every repository, cloud or self-hosted, under a commercial licence. Search across thousands of repositories is the job that page says Sourcegraph is built for. Graphify maps the repositories you point it at, on the machine where you work, and the assistant walks that map. The two can run together. Greptile is hosted review and codebase chat. It indexes your code, and you see pull-request comments plus its own chat. Managed review on every pull request is its core product. graphify prs is on demand. A managed bot that fits your policies is Greptile's job. A graph on the machine fits when the code cannot leave, or when you want each claim auditable. Graphify vs Cursor indexing is the page whose answer is to use both. Cursor's index is embedding similarity inside the editor, automatic, with indexing through Cursor's servers. It surfaces code that looks like what you half remember, and there is nothing to set up. Connected questions are where it runs out. "What breaks if I change this" is a caller of a caller, and the model stitches similar snippets. You also cannot inspect why a snippet was pulled in. Graphify registers as an MCP server, the built-in index stays on, and the agent uses the graph when the question is structural. Graphify vs CodeRabbit acts after the pull request opens: comments in GitHub or GitLab, through a hosted service, once the change is already written. Graphify is for the assistant writing the code, so it can ask what calls this before the edit. Graph-aware review in Graphify is Enterprise, early access, running in your own infrastructure. For a managed bot on every pull request today, that page says a service is the right shape. A common setup is the graph on the machine while code is written, and a hosted reviewer on the pull requests that follow.
